cues.text: Let us turn now to the final theme of this study session: sustaining transformation momentum.
Launching a transformation is one challenge.
Keeping it alive is another.
Many organisations manage an impressive start, with a new platform, a new process, a new set of tools, and then slowly drift back to the old ways of working.
So this section asks a practical question: what makes a transformation sustainable?
The source gives a clear answer.
Transformation becomes sustainable when new behaviours are embedded in five places: workflows, governance, incentives, budgets and skills development.
Let us take these one at a time, because each one is a lock that holds the new behaviour in place.
Workflows are the way work actually moves from person to person.
If the new way of working is not built into the everyday workflow, people will treat it as optional.
Governance covers the decision rights, policies and oversight that say who decides what, and how.
If governance still points to the old process, the new one will always be fighting uphill.
Incentives are what people are rewarded for.
If staff are still measured and rewarded for old behaviours, they will quite rationally keep doing them.
Budgets show what the organisation truly values.
If funding stops after launch, the change starves.
And skills development means people are trained and supported so that they can actually perform the new behaviours with confidence.
So the idea is simple: a new behaviour that lives only in a project plan will fade, but one embedded in workflows, governance, incentives, budgets and skills will last.
The source then turns to leadership.
Leaders must do five things.
First, maintain a clear purpose, so everyone remembers why the change is happening.
Second, celebrate credible short-term wins.
Notice the word credible.
Celebrating real, evidenced progress builds confidence, while celebrating something unproven damages trust.
Third, empower teams, giving them the authority and support to act rather than waiting for permission.
Fourth, update structures, so that reporting lines, roles and teams fit the new way of working.
And fifth, use continual feedback, so leaders keep hearing what is working and what is not.
Now let us look at the second block, which gives us a working routine.
The source calls it a review rhythm, and it has a clear sequence of steps.
Listen to the order.
Step one: monitor agreed KPIs.
KPIs, or key performance indicators, are the measures the organisation has agreed in advance to track progress.
Step two: investigate variance and root causes.
Variance is the gap between what was expected and what actually happened, and the root cause is the underlying reason for that gap, not just the visible symptom.
Step three: select an improvement.
Step four: assign ownership, so a named person or team is accountable.
Step five: implement.
Step six: measure results, to check whether the improvement worked.
And step seven: revise, using what was learned.
Then the rhythm begins again.
So it is a loop, not a one-off event: monitor, investigate, select, assign, implement, measure, revise.
The source adds several balancing principles.
First, balance short-term performance with capability-building and ethical controls.
An organisation that chases only this quarter's numbers may neglect the skills it needs for the future, or cut corners on ethics.
Sustained transformation needs all three held together: results now, capabilities for later, and ethical controls throughout.
Second, the source asks us to maintain training, documentation, succession, communities of practice and transparent lessons.
Training keeps skills current as people join and technology changes.
Documentation preserves how things are done, so knowledge does not live only in individual heads.
Succession means planning who will take over key roles, so momentum survives when leaders or specialists move on.
Communities of practice are groups of people who share a professional interest and learn from each other across team boundaries.
And transparent lessons means sharing what was learned openly, including from things that did not work, so others do not repeat the same mistakes.
Third, the source warns us to avoid change fatigue.
This is the exhaustion people feel when too many changes arrive at once, or never seem to end.

The source gives two remedies: sequence initiatives, meaning spread them in a sensible order rather than launching everything together, and remove obsolete processes, so people are not forced to carry old and new ways of working at the same time.
The final block gives us three diagnostic examples.
They teach one habit: look beneath a headline metric before drawing conclusions.
Example one.
If adoption is high but customer satisfaction falls, investigate experience quality rather than congratulating the rollout.
Adoption only tells you that people are using the new system.
It does not tell you whether the experience is good.
High use with falling satisfaction suggests something about the quality of the experience is wrong, and that deserves investigation, not applause.
Example two.
If deployment frequency rises but outages increase, improve testing and release controls.
Deployment frequency measures how often new software changes are released.
Releasing faster looks like progress, but if outages rise at the same time, changes are reaching users without enough checking.
The source's remedy is to strengthen testing and release controls.
Example three.
If innovation spending rises without outcomes, review portfolio hypotheses and decision gates.
A portfolio is the collection of innovation projects, each resting on hypotheses, which are assumptions about what will create value.
Decision gates are checkpoints where leaders decide whether to continue, change or stop a project.
If money is rising but results are not, the organisation should revisit those hypotheses and check whether its gates are working.
Let us pull this together.
Sustaining momentum means embedding new behaviours in workflows, governance, incentives, budgets and skills.
It means leaders who keep purpose clear, celebrate credible wins, empower teams, update structures and listen through feedback.

It means a disciplined review rhythm, a balance between short-term performance, capability and ethics, protection against change fatigue, and the habit of questioning any metric that looks good while a related one gets worse.
